title: Belfast to Westminster Abbey: the Absolute Scale, the Atlantic Cable, and the Knotted Ether
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Belfast and the House of the Mathematician

stops.name: Belfast, birth in College Square East
stops.campa: William Thomson is born in a house in College Square East, hard by the Royal Belfast Academical Institution where his father James teaches mathematics and engineering to the sons of the linen merchants. He is the fourth of seven children, a delicate boy in a house ruled by figures and diagrams. James Thomson, self-made out of an Ulster farm, has resolved that his sons will not merely learn mathematics but live inside it, and the discipline of that resolve will outlast the father by seventy years, carried first to Glasgow and then round the whole compassed earth by cable and calculation.
suggested_refs: The birthplace plaque at College Square East, Belfast, marking the house of James Thomson
sources: Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson, Baron Kelvin of Largs (1910)
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire: A Biographical Study of Lord Kelvin (1989)

stops.name: Belfast, the death of Margaret Gardner Thomson
stops.campa: William's mother, Margaret Gardner, dies when he is six years old, leaving James Thomson alone with seven children and the whole of their upbringing. The father does not remarry; he takes the education of William and his elder brother James wholly into his own hands, tutoring them at his own table with a rigor that will mark both boys for life. The household becomes a small academy of two pupils and one exacting master, its curriculum mathematics, its discipline unbroken attention, and its only holiday the annual family excursion to the Continent to see waterfalls, glaciers, and instruments.
suggested_refs: James Thomson's manuscript notebooks of home instruction, University of Glasgow archives
sources: Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson, Baron Kelvin of Largs (1910)
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)

stops.name: Glasgow, the family removes to the College
stops.campa: James Thomson is elected Professor of Mathematics at the University of Glasgow, and the whole household migrates from Belfast to the college on the High Street, then still a cluster of medieval-looking courts before the move west to Gilmorehill. The two eldest boys, James and William, are entered as students of their own father's university at an age when other children are still in the nursery. The College becomes literally their home: they live within its walls, attend its logic and Greek and mathematics classes, and grow up thinking of a university as a family's ordinary furniture.
suggested_refs: The Old College on Glasgow's High Street, demolished after the university's 1870 removal to Gilmorehill
sources: Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)
University of Glasgow, 'Lord Kelvin 200' commemorative history

stops.name: Glasgow, matriculation at the University, aged ten
stops.campa: At ten years old William is formally entered on the matriculation roll of the University of Glasgow, sitting in classes of young men twice his age. He wins prizes in Latin, Greek, astronomy, and natural philosophy through his teens, but it is the mathematics and the physical sciences that hold him: he reads far beyond the set texts, borrowing what the college library and his father's shelves can supply. Already the family jokes that he thinks in equations the way other boys think in games, and that a blackboard is his native element.
suggested_refs: The matriculation album of the University of Glasgow, session 1834-35
sources: Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Thomson (1824-1907)'

stops.name: Glasgow, the Essay on the Figure of the Earth
stops.campa: In the astronomy class of session 1839-40, fifteen-year-old William submits an essay on the figure of the Earth so mathematically accomplished that the professor, doubting a boy could have written it unaided, at first withholds the prize. It is finally awarded, a gold medal, and the essay's methods, on the mechanics of rotating, self-gravitating bodies, will occupy Thomson's mind on and off for the rest of his career, a problem he returns to in moments of personal difficulty as another man might return to prayer or verse.
suggested_refs: The 1839-40 astronomy class gold medal, University of Glasgow prize records
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Thomson (1824-1907)'
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: Glasgow, reading Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur
stops.campa: At the end of the session William reads Jean-Baptiste Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur and is transformed by it: a mathematics of heat flow built on differential equations of a beauty he has met nowhere else. British mathematicians of the older school, suspicious of Fourier's series, are still attacking the book; the sixteen-year-old writes and publishes, under the signature 'P.Q.R.', his first papers in its defence. The taste for continental analysis fixed in him this summer, married to heat and to Carnot's engines, will in eight years yield the absolute scale that bears his later name.
suggested_refs: Fourier, Théorie analytique de la chaleur (1822), the volume that converted the young Thomson
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Thomson (1824-1907)'
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)

stops.name: Cambridge, matriculation at Peterhouse
stops.campa: William enters Peterhouse, the oldest and smallest of the Cambridge colleges, in the Michaelmas term of 1841. He has come already reading Fourier and Laplace, so far ahead of the Tripos syllabus that his private coach must slow him down rather than push him on. He rows, plays whist, edits and writes for the newly founded Cambridge Mathematical Journal, and keeps up, through it all, an unbroken correspondence with his father in Glasgow, who tracks every examination and every friendship with the same close attention he once gave the boy's Latin.
suggested_refs: Peterhouse, Cambridge, Thomson's college of matriculation and later fellowship
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Thomson (1824-1907)'
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: Cambridge, the Colquhoun Sculls
stops.campa: William wins the Colquhoun Sculls, the university's premier single-boat race on the Cam, one of the few undergraduates of his year to combine first-rank mathematics with a rowing man's physique and nerve. He keeps a scull, a French horn, and a stack of mathematical journals in the same rooms, and friends of this period remember him as tirelessly sociable rather than the popular caricature of the isolated genius: he organizes concerts, edits a journal, and trains on the river before returning to work through the night on unsolved problems in electricity and heat.
suggested_refs: The Colquhoun Sculls trophy, Cambridge University Boat Club, awarded annually since 1837
sources: Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)

stops.name: Cambridge, the founding of the University Musical Society
stops.campa: Among the undergraduates who found the Cambridge University Musical Society, William gives his evenings to concerts and part-singing with the same appetite he gives his mornings to Green's and Fourier's mathematics. He plays the French horn indifferently but with enthusiasm, and will keep a taste for music, and later for the sea, as the two disciplines outside mathematics that never leave him. Classmates already sense in him something unusual: a mind that treats a symphony, a scull-race, and a partial differential equation as parts of one continuous pleasure.
suggested_refs: The Cambridge University Musical Society, founded 1843, still active
sources: Cambridge University Musical Society, institutional history
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: Cambridge, Second Wrangler and the Smith's Prize
stops.campa: Through twelve days of written examination in the Senate House, William is placed Second Wrangler, behind Stephen Parkinson of St John's, a result his friends and later historians alike call an accident of the Tripos's peculiar scoring rather than a true measure of the two men. A week later the university corrects itself: in the Smith's Prize examination, judged by different examiners on deeper mathematical ground, Thomson is placed unambiguously first. Within months he is elected a Fellow of Peterhouse, the college's youngest in memory.
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Mathematical Tripos results board, January 1845, Senate House
sources: Stephen Parkinson, William Thomson and the Tripos, MacTutor archive essay
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: Cambridge, the recovery of George Green's forgotten Essay
stops.campa: Preparing to leave for Paris, William hears a chance mention of an obscure 1828 pamphlet by the miller-mathematician George Green, dead four years and almost unknown. No copy can be found in the Cambridge booksellers or the college libraries; at last a fellow of Caius produces one from his own shelves. Reading it, Thomson recognizes at once a theory of potential far ahead of its time, buried by Green's total obscurity. He carries the little book to Paris in his luggage, determined that Liouville and the French mathematicians will not let it die a second time.
suggested_refs: George Green, An Essay on the Application of Mathematical Analysis to the Theories of Electricity and Magnetism (Nottingham, 1828)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Green (mathematician)'
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: Paris, the laboratory of Henri Victor Regnault
stops.campa: Thomson spends the autumn of 1845 working in the laboratory of Henri Victor Regnault at the Collège de France, the most exact experimental physicist in Europe, whose measurements of the properties of steam and gases underlie every steam engine's design. Here the Cambridge mathematician, until now a creature of pure analysis, learns for the first time the discipline of the instrument bench: the endless patience of calibration, the distrust of any number not independently checked. It is Regnault's painstaking data on gases that Thomson will use, three years later, to calculate an absolute scale of temperature founded on theory rather than on the accident of mercury or water.
suggested_refs: Regnault's laboratory apparatus at the Collège de France, models preserved in French scientific-instrument collections
sources: Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Thomson (1824-1907)'

stops.name: Paris, Green's Essay laid before Liouville and Sturm
stops.campa: Thomson shows the recovered pamphlet of George Green to Joseph Liouville and Charles-François Sturm, the leading mathematical physicists of Paris, and its unlooked-for depth causes something close to a sensation among men who had never heard the dead Englishman's name. Thomson arranges for the Essay to be reprinted in Crelle's Journal, the standard organ of continental mathematics, over the following years, so that a miller's son who taught himself potential theory in a Nottingham bakehouse is at last read where the mathematics of the age is actually made and judged.
suggested_refs: Crelle's Journal (Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik), where Green's Essay was serially reprinted
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Green (mathematician)'
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: Glasgow, election to the Chair of Natural Philosophy
stops.campa: At twenty-two, fresh from Cambridge and Paris, William Thomson is elected Professor of Natural Philosophy at the University of Glasgow, the chair his own father has coached him for since boyhood. He will hold it for fifty-three years without a break, refusing repeated invitations to Cambridge, Oxford, and abroad. Colleagues expect a brilliant but conventional lecturer; instead the young professor immediately begins to drag the whole apparatus of experimental physics, batteries, coils, gauges, and eventually a teaching laboratory, into a curriculum that until now has been chalk and blackboard only.
suggested_refs: The Natural Philosophy classroom of the Old College, Glasgow, Thomson's first lecture hall
sources: University of Glasgow, 'Lord Kelvin 200' commemorative history
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)

stops.name: Glasgow, the founding of the first teaching laboratory
stops.campa: In a disused wine cellar under the old college, Thomson sets up what becomes recognized as the first undergraduate teaching laboratory of experimental physics in Britain, where students measure rather than merely watch. He buys instruments out of his own salary, badgers instrument-makers for improvements, and drills his classes in the same discipline of exact numbers he learned from Regnault in Paris. Decades later, students recall the cellar's damp and clutter with real affection: it is where natural philosophy in Scotland stops being a lecture and starts being a practice of the hands.
suggested_refs: The wine-cellar laboratory of the Old College, Glasgow, forerunner of the modern teaching laboratory
sources: University of Glasgow, 'Lord Kelvin 200' commemorative history
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)

stops.name: Oxford, the meeting with James Prescott Joule
stops.campa: At the British Association meeting in Oxford, a young Manchester brewer named James Prescott Joule reads a paper claiming to have measured, with a paddle-wheel churning water in an insulated can, the exact mechanical equivalent of heat. Most of the assembled savants ignore it as amateur curiosity; Thomson alone rises from the audience to question Joule closely, half-convinced the brewer must be wrong, wholly unable to stop thinking about it afterward. He will spend the rest of the year unlearning the caloric theory of heat he was raised on, and starting the friendship that will remake thermodynamics.
suggested_refs: Joule's paddle-wheel apparatus for measuring the mechanical equivalent of heat, Science Museum, London
sources: Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'William Thomson (1824-1907)'

stops.name: Chamonix, the waterfall experiment
stops.campa: By pure chance, walking in the valley of Chamonix that same summer, Thomson meets Joule again, thermometer in hand, on his honeymoon, still hunting for proof of his theory in the natural world. The two men climb together to a waterfall on the Sallanches road and attempt, half in earnest and half as a shared joke against the whole learned world, to measure whether water falling a great height arrives at the bottom warmer than it left the top, exactly as Joule's mechanical-equivalent theory predicts it must. The spray defeats the thermometer, but not the friendship, nor the theory.
suggested_refs: The Chamonix valley and the Sallanches waterfall, scene of the improvised thermometer experiment
sources: Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)
Physics World, 'William Thomson: king of Victorian physics'

stops.name: Glasgow, 'On an Absolute Thermometric Scale'
stops.campa: Working from Carnot's theory of the motive power of heat and from Regnault's Paris data on gases, Thomson publishes a scale of temperature that depends on no particular substance, water, mercury, or air, but on the theoretical behaviour of an ideal heat engine. He fixes its zero at the point where a gas's pressure would vanish altogether: minus 273 degrees on the old Celsius scale, a cold no vessel on Earth has ever reached but which the mathematics demands as an absolute floor beneath all possible temperature.
stops.quote: The characteristic property of the scale which I now propose is, that all degrees have the same value; that is, that a unit of heat descending from a body A at the temperature T° of this scale, to a body B at the temperature (T-1)°, would give out the same mechanical effect, whatever be the number T.
stops.quote_source: 'On an Absolute Thermometric Scale Founded on Carnot's Theory of the Motive Power of Heat', Philosophical Magazine (1848)
suggested_refs: The Kelvin scale, SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, zeroed at Thomson's absolute zero
sources: William Thomson, 'On an Absolute Thermometric Scale' (1848)
ChemistryViews, 'Lord Kelvin, the Coldest Possible Temperature'

stops.name: Glasgow, 'On the Dynamical Theory of Heat'
stops.campa: Reading before the Royal Society of Edinburgh, Thomson lays out the dynamical theory of heat that reconciles Carnot's engine theory with Joule's mechanical equivalent, work he has been turning over since Oxford and Chamonix. In the same paper he states, independently of but consistent with Clausius on the Continent, the principle that will stand as the second law of thermodynamics: no engine, however perfect, can draw useful work from heat alone without some of that heat passing to a colder body. It becomes the axiom on which every steam engine, every refrigerator, and eventually every theory of the universe's slow decay will be built.
stops.quote: It is impossible, by means of inanimate material agency, to derive mechanical effect from any portion of matter by cooling it below the temperature of the coldest of the surrounding objects.
stops.quote_source: 'On the Dynamical Theory of Heat', Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (1851)
suggested_refs: Thomson's 1851 statement of the second law of thermodynamics, alongside Clausius's contemporary formulation
sources: William Thomson, 'On the Dynamical Theory of Heat' (1851)
Stephen Wolfram, 'How Did We Get Here? The Tangled History of the Second Law of Thermodynamics'

stops.name: Thornliebank, marriage to Margaret Crum
stops.campa: William marries Margaret Crum, daughter of the chemist and calico-printer Walter Crum of Thornliebank, a childhood friend of the family from summers on the Clyde. She is delicate in health from the start of the marriage, and will remain so for its whole eighteen years, following her husband on cable expeditions and instrument trials when she is well enough and waiting anxiously at Glasgow when she is not. Their household becomes, like his laboratory, an extension of the work: dinner-table talk of galvanometers and gutta-percha insulation, guests drawn from half the learned societies of Europe.
suggested_refs: Thornliebank House, near Glasgow, the Crum family seat
sources: Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)

stops.name: Glasgow, appointment as director of the Atlantic Telegraph Company
stops.campa: Cyrus Field's newly formed Atlantic Telegraph Company enlists Thomson as one of its scientific directors, drawn by his 1855 theoretical paper proving that a signal sent down a long submarine cable spreads and slows in proportion to the square of the cable's length, the 'law of squares' that the company's own chief electrician, Wildman Whitehouse, publicly disputes and privately ignores. Thomson accepts unpaid, buys shares he can ill afford, and commits himself for the next decade to a wager that a wire two thousand four hundred miles long can be made to speak across an ocean floor no one has properly sounded.
suggested_refs: Thomson's 1855 paper on signal retardation in submarine cables, the theoretical basis of the whole enterprise
sources: Jakob Nebeker, 'Science and Technology: Lord Kelvin's Atlantic Cable'
Crosbie Smith & M. Norton Wise, Energy and Empire (1989)

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, the cable snaps on the first expedition
stops.campa: Six days out from Valentia, with the Agamemnon and the Niagara paying out cable from opposite ends toward mid-ocean, a wave pitches the Niagara and a brake is clapped on too hard: the cable parts and two miles of copper and gutta-percha spool away to the sea floor, three hundred and eighty miles of the expedition's work lost in an instant. Thomson, aboard as scientific adviser, watches the whole apparatus of the enterprise, ships, money, reputation, sink with it. The company does not abandon the project; it orders more cable and books the ships again for the following summer.
suggested_refs: The 1857 Atlantic Telegraph expedition log, recording the cable's parting at 3:45 a.m.
sources: PBS American Experience, 'Attempts to Lay the Transatlantic Cable'
Jakob Nebeker, 'Science and Technology: Lord Kelvin's Atlantic Cable'

stops.name: Glasgow, the invention of the mirror galvanometer
stops.campa: Over the winter following the failure, Thomson builds the instrument on which the whole project's second attempt will turn: a tiny mirror, no bigger than a shirt button, cemented to a magnetized needle and suspended within a coil, so that a beam of lamplight reflected off it swings across a graduated scale at the faintest current a submarine cable can carry. Where Whitehouse's crude receivers demand currents strong enough to burn the insulation, Thomson's mirror reads a signal too weak to feel. It is the instrument, more than any other single object, that will make transoceanic telegraphy possible.
suggested_refs: Thomson's mirror galvanometer, examples preserved at the Science Museum, London, and the Grinnell College Physics Museum
sources: Grinnell College Physics Museum, 'Thomson's Mirror Galvanometer'
Wikipedia, 'Mirror galvanometer'

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, the mid-ocean splice
stops.campa: The Agamemnon and the Niagara meet at an agreed point in mid-Atlantic, splice their two cable-ends together, and turn away from each other, one steaming toward Valentia in Ireland, the other toward Trinity Bay in Newfoundland, paying out wire behind them at a steady four miles an hour. Thomson stands watch over the mirror galvanometer through storms that nearly founder the Agamemnon in the Bay of Biscay before the ships have even reached the splice point, reading the faint returning pulses that tell him, hour by hour, that the cable beneath them is still whole.
suggested_refs: The mid-ocean splice point of 1858, roughly 52°N 33°W, marked on Atlantic cable charts
sources: Science Museum, 'How perseverance laid the first transatlantic telegraph cable'
IEEE Spectrum, 'The First Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Was a Bold, Beautiful Failure'

stops.name: Valentia and Trinity Bay, the cable speaks and then falls silent
stops.campa: On the fifth of August both shore ends land safely, and within days messages cross the ocean in minutes that once took ships eleven days, Queen Victoria's ninety-eight-word greeting to President Buchanan among the first. But Whitehouse, distrusting Thomson's delicate mirror, insists on driving the line with induction coils at thousands of volts to force a stronger signal through; within weeks the excess current burns through the gutta-percha insulation deep under the Atlantic, and by early September the cable that joined two continents has gone permanently silent, its brief triumph curdling into public humiliation for the whole enterprise.
suggested_refs: Queen Victoria's 1858 message to President Buchanan, the cable's most famous transmission before its failure
sources: Scientific American, 'The Atlantic Cable' (21 August 1858)
IEEE Spectrum, 'The First Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Was a Bold, Beautiful Failure'

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, the Great Eastern loses the 1865 cable
stops.campa: Seven years and a civil war later, the project resumes with Brunel's vast iron steamship the Great Eastern, the only vessel afloat large enough to carry an entire ocean's length of cable in one hold. Some twelve hundred miles out and roughly six hundred short of Newfoundland, the cable parts again and sinks in water two and a half miles deep. Thomson and the crew spend days dragging grapples across the sea floor trying to recover the lost end, hauling it twice to within sight of the surface before the strain snaps the recovery rope each time, and at last the ship turns back empty-handed.
suggested_refs: SS Great Eastern, Brunel's iron steamship, sole vessel of the era able to carry the whole Atlantic cable
sources: IET Archives, 'The Transatlantic Telegraph Cables 1865-1866'
PBS American Experience, 'Attempts to Lay the Transatlantic Cable'

stops.name: Heart's Content, Newfoundland, the cable completed
stops.campa: The Great Eastern sails again on the thirteenth of July with a new and stronger cable, and this time nothing parts: on the twenty-seventh she steams into Heart's Content, Newfoundland, and the shore end is landed to cheering crowds. Thomson's mirror galvanometer reads a clean signal from Valentia within the hour. For the first time a transatlantic cable holds, works, and keeps working; the eleven-day Atlantic crossing by fastest steamer is compressed, for messages, to a matter of minutes, and the world Thomson's generation is building suddenly has a nervous system.
suggested_refs: The 1866 cable terminus at Heart's Content, Newfoundland, now the Cable Station Provincial Historic Site
sources: Victorian Web, 'The Laying of Submarine Cable: the Triumph of Brunel's Great Eastern'
IET Archives, 'The Transatlantic Telegraph Cables 1865-1866'

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, the 1865 cable grappled up from the deep
stops.campa: Having landed one working cable, the Great Eastern turns back to the position, fixed the year before by careful navigation, where the 1865 line was lost, and after three weeks and some thirty attempts at grappling two and a half miles down, the ship's crew at last raises the year-old cable to the surface, splices in a new shore length, and finds it, after twelve months on the ocean floor, still able to carry a signal. Two working cables now cross the Atlantic where none had survived a fortnight eight years before; the ocean has, at the second real attempt, been made to keep a promise.
suggested_refs: Atlantic-cable.com, 'Recovery of the Lost Cable, 1866', contemporary account of the grapple
sources: Atlantic-cable.com, 'Recovery of the Lost Cable, 1866'
Victorian Web, 'The Laying of Submarine Cable'

stops.name: Windsor, the knighthood
stops.campa: Queen Victoria knights William Thomson at Windsor for his part in the cable's success, one honour among many that year, but the one he will remember by taking a title from it a quarter-century later. He accepts it as recognition less of his own theory than of a whole decade's collective stubbornness, engineers, cable-layers, ships' captains, and the instrument on the mirror-lit table that finally let a whisper of current cross two thousand miles of ocean and be heard.
suggested_refs: Windsor Castle, site of the 1866 knighthood ceremony
sources: Historic UK, 'Sir William Thomson, Baron Kelvin of Largs'
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

segments.name: The Vortex Atom and the Knots

stops.name: Edinburgh, Tait's smoke-ring apparatus
stops.campa: Thomson's old Cambridge friend Peter Guthrie Tait, now professor at Edinburgh, builds a wooden box with a drum-skin at one end and a round hole at the other, and by thumping the drum sends smoke rings drifting and colliding across the lecture room. Thomson, watching, sees the rings bounce off one another as though made of something almost solid, spin without unraveling, and hold their shape across a room. Where others see a parlour trick, he sees, arriving all at once, an answer to the oldest of physical questions: what an atom is, and why it does not simply fall apart.
suggested_refs: Tait's smoke-ring apparatus, reconstructions preserved in the history-of-physics collections at Edinburgh
sources: MIT, 'Peter Guthrie Tait' (history of knot theory archive)
Medium, 'Kelvin's Brilliant Vortex Atom'

stops.name: Edinburgh, 'On Vortex Atoms'
stops.campa: Thomson reads to the Royal Society of Edinburgh a paper proposing that every atom of every element is not a hard indivisible pellet but a vortex ring, a closed loop of rotating motion knotted permanently into Helmholtz's perfect, frictionless ether. Such a knot, once tied in a fluid without viscosity, can be neither created nor destroyed except by an act outside nature altogether; its particular knotting, its particular twist, determines which element it is. The theory will later be shown false, the ether itself does not exist, but the paper leaves behind a permanent gift: the mathematical study of knots as objects in their own right.
stops.quote: Helmholtz's rings are the only true atoms... To generate or to destroy 'Wirbelbewegung' in a perfect fluid can only be an act of creative power.
stops.quote_source: 'On Vortex Atoms', Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, vol. 6 (1867)
suggested_refs: Helmholtz's 1858 paper on vortex motion, the theoretical foundation Thomson builds on
corpus essay 209, 'Thread and Wheel', on the deep kinship of cordage, spin, and chirality
sources: William Thomson, 'On Vortex Atoms' (1867)
3 Quarks Daily, 'Lord Kelvin and his Atomic Vortices'

stops.name: Edinburgh, the completed table of knots
stops.campa: Set going by Thomson's vortex-atom theory, Tait spends the better part of two decades trying to enumerate, by hand and by an almost obsessive patience, every distinct way a closed loop of string can be knotted, first to seven crossings, then, with the amateur mathematician Thomas Kirkman supplying projections of ever greater complexity, to ten. In September 1885 the finished tables, hundreds of knots sorted and classified with a rigor no one has attempted before, are printed at last: correct, complete, and the founding document of what will become a whole branch of mathematics, knot theory, born from an atom theory that turned out to be wrong about the physics and right about the knots.
suggested_refs: Tait's 1885 tables of knots up to ten crossings, foundational document of knot theory
corpus essay 207, 'Hebraic Knots', on the parallel life of cordage as sacred and mnemonic form
sources: MIT, 'Peter Guthrie Tait' (history of knot theory archive)
History of Knot Theory from Gauss to Jones (Springer, 2023)

stops.name: Glasgow, 'On the Secular Cooling of the Earth'
stops.campa: Thomson publishes his celebrated calculation of the Earth's age, treating the planet as a body that began wholly molten and has been losing heat by conduction ever since, its present underground temperature gradient the fossil record of that cooling. From Fourier's own equations for heat flow, the same mathematics he read as a boy of sixteen, he derives a bracket of time within which the Earth's crust must have solidified: not less than twenty million years, not more than four hundred million. Geologists accustomed to unlimited time, and the new Darwinians who need it for natural selection to work its slow effects, receive the number as an unwelcome ultimatum from a science that claims the authority of physical law.
stops.quote: I think we may with much probability say that the consolidation cannot have taken place less than 20,000,000 years ago, or we should have more underground heat than we actually have, nor more than 400,000,000 years ago, or we should not have so much as the least observed underground increment of temperature.
stops.quote_source: 'On the Secular Cooling of the Earth', Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (1862)
suggested_refs: Kelvin's cooling-Earth model, later superseded by the discovery of radioactive heating
sources: William Thomson, 'On the Secular Cooling of the Earth' (1862)
American Scientist, 'Kelvin, Perry and the Age of the Earth'

stops.name: Glasgow, the address 'On Geological Time'
stops.campa: Addressing the Glasgow Geological Society, Thomson presses the argument further, and further into open conflict with the uniformitarian geology of Lyell and the biology of Darwin, both of which assume an Earth old enough to make gradual, unhurried change the only engine needed. He does not deny natural selection outright, but insists that whatever process shapes species, it must fit inside a physically bounded span of years, not an unlimited one borrowed from an older and less rigorous science. Huxley, Darwin's fiercest public defender, will spend years searching for a flaw in the physicist's mathematics rather than conceding the geologists' oldest working assumption.
suggested_refs: T.H. Huxley's 1869 presidential address to the Geological Society, answering Thomson's challenge
sources: American Scientist, 'Kelvin, Perry and the Age of the Earth'
Science & Education, 'Lord Kelvin and the Age-of-the-Earth Debate: A Dramatization'

stops.name: Glasgow, the dispute unresolved into old age
stops.campa: By the 1890s Thomson, now Lord Kelvin, has narrowed his own estimate still further, to somewhere between twenty and forty million years, squeezing the geologists and the Darwinians into an ever tighter span. His former student John Perry publishes a careful rebuttal, arguing that convection inside the Earth, not simple conduction, would keep it far hotter for far longer than Kelvin's model allows; Kelvin does not yield the point in his lifetime. Neither man yet knows that the Earth's interior carries its own inexhaustible furnace of radioactive decay, undiscovered heat that will, within a decade of Kelvin's death, quietly dissolve the whole ultimatum and hand geology back its deep time.
suggested_refs: John Perry's 1895 letters to Nature challenging Kelvin's conduction-only model of the Earth's interior
sources: American Scientist, 'Kelvin, Perry and the Age of the Earth'
Science & Education, 'Lord Kelvin and the Age-of-the-Earth Debate: A Dramatization'

segments.name: Baron Kelvin, the Lalla Rookh, and Largs

stops.name: Firth of Clyde, the purchase of the Lalla Rookh
stops.campa: Margaret Thomson dies in June 1870 after a long decline, and three months later, still in grief, William buys the hundred-and-twenty-six-ton schooner-yacht Lalla Rookh and begins a second life on the water that will last the rest of his years. He fits her out as a floating laboratory, testing his own inventions, an improved mariner's compass, sounding equipment for measuring the ocean floor at speed, against the real conditions of open sea that no tank or bench can reproduce. Half of his seventy patents are born or proved aboard her decks off the Scottish coast and, later, off Madeira.
suggested_refs: The Lalla Rookh, Thomson's schooner-yacht and seagoing instrument laboratory
sources: National Academies Press, Degrees Kelvin: A Tale of Genius, Invention, and Tragedy (2004)
University of Glasgow, 'Lord Kelvin 200' commemorative history

stops.name: Madeira, marriage to Frances Anna Blandy
stops.campa: A cable fault the year before had stranded Thomson's ship off Madeira for a fortnight, during which the island's wealthiest landowner, Charles Blandy, entertained the scientific adviser and his family were his guests. William, two days short of his fiftieth birthday, sails the Lalla Rookh back to the island the following spring and marries Blandy's daughter Fanny, thirty-six years old, in the British Consular Chapel at Funchal. She will be, for the rest of his life, his steadiest companion on every cable expedition, every yacht cruise, and every winter of controversy over the age of the Earth.
suggested_refs: The British Consular Chapel (Church of the Holy Trinity), Funchal, Madeira, site of the 1874 wedding
sources: National Academies Press, Degrees Kelvin (2004)
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: London, 'Electrical Units of Measurement'
stops.campa: Lecturing to the Institution of Civil Engineers, Thomson states as a single memorable sentence the working creed of his whole scientific life: that a science worth the name begins in measurement and number, and that anything not yet reducible to number is only the beginning, not the substance, of knowledge. It is the same conviction, restated for engineers rather than physicists, that drove the mirror galvanometer, the absolute thermometric scale, and the improved compass alike: not mathematics for its own elegant sake, but mathematics harnessed to an instrument that can be read.
stops.quote: When you can measure what you are speaking about, and express it in numbers, you know something about it; but when you cannot measure it, when you cannot express it in numbers, your knowledge is of a meagre and unsatisfactory kind: it may be the beginning of knowledge, but you have scarcely, in your thoughts, advanced to the stage of science, whatever the matter may be.
stops.quote_source: 'Electrical Units of Measurement', lecture to the Institution of Civil Engineers (3 May 1883), Popular Lectures and Addresses (1889)
suggested_refs: Popular Lectures and Addresses, vol. 1 (1889), collecting Thomson's public lectures
sources: WIST Quotations, 'Kelvin (Lord) — Electrical Units of Measurement'
William Thomson, Popular Lectures and Addresses (1889)

stops.name: London, the presidency of the Royal Society
stops.campa: Thomson is elected President of the Royal Society, the summit of institutional honour available to a British man of science, a post he will hold for five years while continuing, without pause, his Glasgow lectures, his cable consulting, and his instrument patents. He presides over the Society through a decade in which the physics he was trained in, mechanical, deterministic, built on ether and absolute certainty, is beginning, though he does not yet fully see it, to show its first cracks: unexplained spectral lines, an ether that stubbornly refuses to be detected, radiations no one predicted.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's presidential chair, Burlington House, London
sources: The Royal Society, list of past presidents
Silvanus P. Thompson, The Life of William Thomson (1910)

stops.name: London, elevation to the peerage as Baron Kelvin
stops.campa: Queen Victoria raises William Thomson to the peerage as Baron Kelvin of Largs, in the county of Ayr, the first scientist ever elevated to the House of Lords for scientific work alone rather than for wealth or inherited rank. He takes his title, as he took his knighthood's memory, from the small river Kelvin that runs through the grounds of his own university at Glasgow: a working man's chair, not a landed estate, is the thing he chooses to be permanently named after. In the Lords he will speak rarely, but always on questions of science, patents, and imperial cable communication.
suggested_refs: The River Kelvin, Glasgow, source of the peerage title
sources: Chemistry World, 'The first scientific baron'
Historic UK, 'Sir William Thomson, Baron Kelvin of Largs'

stops.name: Glasgow, retirement from the Chair after fifty-three years
stops.campa: In his seventy-fifth year, Kelvin retires from the Chair of Natural Philosophy at Glasgow, the same chair he was elected to at twenty-two, held continuously for fifty-three years without once accepting an offer to leave for a grander post elsewhere. He immediately re-enrols, at the university's invitation, as a research student under his own successor, unwilling simply to stop working at a bench he has occupied longer than most of his colleagues have been alive. The laboratory he built in a disused wine cellar has by now grown into a proper department with its own building; the boy who matriculated at ten leaves the university an old man who never really left it at all.
suggested_refs: The Kelvin Building, University of Glasgow, raised in his honour
sources: University of Glasgow, 'Lord Kelvin 200' commemorative history
Physics World, 'William Thomson: king of Victorian physics'

stops.name: London, 'Nineteenth-Century Clouds over the Dynamical Theory of Heat and Light'
stops.campa: Before the Royal Institution, seventy-five years old, Kelvin surveys the whole edifice of classical mechanical physics that has been his life's instrument, heat, light, ether, motion, and names two remaining difficulties that will not be forced into it: the stubborn failure of every experiment to detect the Earth's motion through the ether, and the wrong prediction every existing theory makes for the colour of radiated heat. He calls them, memorably, two clouds. Within five years the first cloud will help produce Einstein's relativity and the second will help produce quantum theory, though Kelvin, dying within the decade, will not live to see either storm break from the clouds he named.
stops.quote: The beauty and clearness of the dynamical theory, which asserts heat and light to be modes of motion, is at present obscured by two clouds.
stops.quote_source: 'Nineteenth-Century Clouds over the Dynamical Theory of Heat and Light', address to the Royal Institution (27 April 1900), published Philosophical Magazine (July 1901)
suggested_refs: The 1900 lecture text, 'Nineteenth-Century Clouds', Royal Institution archive
sources: William Thomson, 'Nineteenth-Century Clouds over the Dynamical Theory of Heat and Light' (1901)
Chad Orzel, 'Kelvin and Michelson and Historical Myths'

stops.name: Netherhall, Largs, the death
stops.campa: Lord Kelvin dies at Netherhall, his house above the Firth of Clyde at Largs, of a severe chill, in his eighty-fourth year, still president of no fewer learned societies than he has ever been, still holding patents still in active use on ships at sea. From the schoolboy who thought in Fourier's equations to the Baron who named the clouds over physics, the arc closes within sight of the same water the Lalla Rookh once sailed, and within an afternoon's journey of the Glasgow chair he held for more than half a century.
suggested_refs: Netherhall, Largs, Kelvin's house on the Firth of Clyde, his final home
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Times obituary of William Thomson'
Westminster Abbey, 'William Thomson, Lord Kelvin'

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, burial beside Newton
stops.campa: On a dark, cold midwinter day the Royal Society, having asked and been granted the Dean's leave, buries Lord Kelvin in Westminster Abbey, his coffin carried in to Purcell's music for Queen Mary's funeral and out to Chopin's funeral march, ambassadors and cabinet ministers and the whole learned world of Britain in attendance. He is laid to rest in the nave just to the south of the grave of Sir Isaac Newton, absolute zero and absolute space keeping company at last under the same stone floor, the boy who once measured a Scottish waterfall's warmth now measured, permanently, against the man who first wrote down the laws of motion.
suggested_refs: Kelvin's grave in the nave of Westminster Abbey, immediately south of Newton's
sources: Westminster Abbey, 'William Thomson, Lord Kelvin'
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Times obituary of William Thomson'
